name: Diff_Product_1
questiontext:
Find the derivative of the following function evaluated at the point \(c\): \[ f({{CT:0}})={{CT:1}} \frac{{CT:0}}{\sin({{CT:0}})} \] where \[c={{CT:2}}\]

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
generalfeedback:
In order to solve this problem we will have to use the product rule \(\frac{d}{dx}(fg) = \frac{df}{dx}\cdot g+f\cdot\frac{dg}{dx}\) as follows:

Let \(f(x) = {{CT:1}}{{CT:0}}\mbox{ and }g(x) = \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sin({{CT:0}})}\)
\[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle \frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}\left({{CT:3}}\right) &=& \left(\frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}({{CT:4}})\right)\cdot {{CT:5}} + ({{CT:4}})\cdot \left(\frac{d}{d{{CT:0}}}\left({{CT:5}}\right)\right) \\ & =& ({{CT:6}})\cdot {{CT:5}} + ({{CT:4}})\cdot {{CT:7}} \\ &=& {{CT:8}} \end{array}\] Evaluated at {{CT:9}} = {{CT:10}} this yields {{CT:11}}.

on_true.feedback: To differentiate a product use the rule \[\frac{d}{dx}(fg) = \frac{df}{dx}\cdot g+f\cdot\frac{dg}{dx}.\] You cannot get the derivative of a product by multiplying the derivatives.
You appear to have applied the product rule incorrectly. It is \[\frac{df}{dx}\cdot g+f\cdot\frac{dg}{dx},\] not \[f\cdot\frac{df}{dx}+g\cdot\frac{dg}{dx}.\]
